title: Leading Yourself (the part of leadership nobody can do for you)
author: Ian Hallett
summary: In the first of a five-part series on his Leadership Operating System, Ian Hallett argues that leading yourself is the first domain of leadership because the other four depend on it. He opens with Satya Nadella's public misstep on women asking for pay rises and his same-day apology, then grounds the domain in research on managers who seek negative feedback and on expressed humility. The domain has three disciplines, composure, learning and candour, each with five concrete behaviours and a specific action to practise. He offers a three-question weekly self-check: was I calm when it mattered, what did I learn and what will I change, and where was I wrong and did I say so. He lists four ways capable people neglect the domain, then replays the Nadella episode against the checklist. He is frank about the limits, noting that nobody has tested this particular self-check.
points: Hallett frames leading yourself as the first domain because judgement under pressure depends on composure and you cannot develop others if you cannot take feedback yourself.
Research he cites found that managers who sought negative feedback were rated more effective than those who sought praise, and that expressed humility predicted performance and lower team turnover.
The three questions of the self-check, covering composure, learning and candour, can be answered in three lines each in writing after a testing moment or once a week.
Each of the fifteen behaviours comes with a concrete action, such as spending the first thirty seconds on bad news asking what happened, what is certain and what is needed from you.
He warns that private lessons and nightly self-criticism feel like leading yourself but change nothing the team can see, because only visible behaviour counts.
quotes: Your team works with your habits every day, so leading yourself is the first thing you do for them.
Managers who asked for negative feedback were rated more effective. Managers who went looking for praise were rated less effective.
It comes first because the other four domains depend on it. Judgement under pressure depends on composure, and you cannot develop anyone else if you cannot take feedback yourself.
Results got you promoted. Nobody appraised your composure, or asked how often you changed your mind in public. At the next level, people notice those things.
Composure is choosing how you behave before you feel calm enough to. Your team checks it every time they bring you something difficult.
Experience does not turn into learning by itself. Something in your week has to force the lesson out, and this discipline is a set of small routines that do the forcing.
The private lesson. You learn, and you change, and nobody is told. The team goes on working around the old version of you, because the old behaviour is the only evidence they have.
We replay the meeting at night, go over what we should have said, and call it reflection. It feels like leading yourself and changes nothing anyone else can see.
